lesson.title: Spotting the Inside Function
lesson.summary: Correctly identifying the inside function, the expression tucked inside the outer operation, is the single most error prone step in applying the chain rule, and getting it right sets up everything else.
lesson.body:
In a composition f(g(x)), the inner function g(x) is literally what sits inside the outer operation, whatever expression the outer function is applied to. In e^(5x - 2), the inside function is 5x - 2. In ln(x^2 + 7), the inside function is x^2 + 7. In sqrt(9 - x^2), the inside function is 9 - x^2, with the square root wrapped around it as the outer operation. Correctly identifying this inner piece before writing down any derivative is what makes the rest of the chain rule computation go smoothly, since the chain rule formula needs g'(x) as a standalone ingredient, and that piece cannot be found correctly until g(x) itself has been separated cleanly from the rest of the expression.

A reliable strategy is to imagine plugging in a specific number and ask what the very last arithmetic step would be. Whatever gets computed just before that last step is the inside function. For (3x + 1)^4, evaluating at x = 2 means first computing 3(2) + 1 = 7, and only afterward raising that result to the fourth power. The computation done before the final operation, 3x + 1, is the inside function, and the final operation, raising to the fourth power, is left as the outer function.

Apply this to y = ln(x^3 - 4x). The inside function is g(x) = x^3 - 4x, so g'(x) = 3x^2 - 4, and the outer function is f(u) = ln u, so f'(u) = 1/u. The chain rule gives dy/dx = (3x^2 - 4) / (x^3 - 4x). Spot check at x = -1, where the inside function value is (-1) - 4(-1) = -1 + 4 = 3, safely positive so the logarithm is defined. There, g'(-1) = 3(1) - 4 = -1, and the derivative evaluates to -1/3, consistent with plugging x = -1 directly into the formula.

A common trap is misapplying this idea to an expression that is not really a single composition. Consider y = e^(2x) times x^3. This is a product of two separate factors, e^(2x) and x^3, not one function nested inside another as a whole. It would be a mistake to treat the entire expression e^(2x) x^3 as if it were the inside function of some larger operation. The chain rule identification here applies only locally, to the factor e^(2x) alone, where 2x is the inside function; the two factors must then be combined properly with the product rule, not merged into a single inside function spanning the whole product.

A useful habit is to work from the outside in, mentally stripping away the outermost operation, whether that is a power, a root, a logarithm, or an exponential, to reveal whatever remains underneath. Sometimes what remains is a simple polynomial, and the process stops there. Other times what remains is itself another layered expression, which means the stripping process needs to repeat, a situation the nested chain rule handles directly later in this chapter, where identifying the inside function correctly at every layer becomes even more important.
